title: Fourth Person Dies in New York City's Legionnaires' Disease Outbreak
excerpt: The death toll from a Legionnaires' disease cluster on Manhattan's Upper East Side has risen to four, with 76 cases reported, though health officials say the source of the outbreak has been eliminated.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A fourth person has died in the Legionnaires' disease outbreak, totaling 76 cases in NYC.
  • The outbreak source, contaminated cooling towers, has been eliminated through remediation efforts.
  • No new symptoms reported for over a week, but symptoms can appear up to 14 days post-exposure.
  • City Council plans to strengthen cooling tower inspection requirements following the outbreak.

  • A fourth person has died in connection with a Legionnaires' disease cluster on Manhattan's Upper East Side, bringing total cases to 76.
  • Health officials say the source of the outbreak — contaminated building cooling towers — has been eliminated through aggressive remediation.
  • No new symptoms have been reported for over a week, but authorities warn that symptoms can appear up to 14 days after exposure.
  • The City Council is introducing legislation to strengthen cooling tower inspection requirements following the outbreak.

Death Toll Rises as Outbreak Wanes

New York City Health Commissioner Dr. Alister Martin confirmed late Monday that a fourth person had died in connection with the Legionnaires' disease cluster centered on the Upper East Side neighborhoods of Carnegie Hill and Yorkville.

> **"We mourn their passing, and our thoughts are with their family and loved ones."

— Dr."** https://x.com/realTuckFrumper/status/2079567986940113346

"A fourth person has sadly died from Legionnaires' disease on the Upper East Side. We mourn their passing, and our thoughts are with their family and loved ones."

— Dr. Alister Martin, NYC Health Commissioner

As of July 20, the city's Health Department reported 76 total cases from the community outbreak. Seven people remain hospitalised, while 53 patients have been discharged. The first death was announced on Friday, July 17, with the second and third reported over the weekend.

Despite the rising toll, officials expressed confidence that the worst of the outbreak has passed. Martin said his department had not identified anyone with new symptoms for more than a week and was not seeing concerning trends in emergency department surveillance data.

Cooling Towers Identified as Source

Investigators traced the outbreak to Legionella bacteria found in building cooling towers — rooftop units that can disperse contaminated water droplets into the air, which people then inhale. The affected area spans three zip codes: 10028, 10128 and 10075.

Health officials ordered 76 buildings with cooling towers in the affected zone to undergo emergency remediation and disinfect their systems beginning July 14. All 76 buildings have confirmed they completed the required work.

"We believe the source of exposure has likely been eliminated due to our aggressive remediation and enforcement efforts. We will continue inspecting every cooling tower that tested positive and will hold accountable any owner who fails to comply with our public health laws."

— NYC Health Department Statement

City officials, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, attributed the containment to the "aggressive strategy of early testing, enforcement, and remediation." However, the outbreak has already surpassed the threshold that typically triggers heightened public concern in the city.

Council Pushes for Tougher Oversight

City Council Speaker Julie Menin announced plans to introduce legislation requiring the city to proactively identify cooling towers that building owners failed to test for Legionella bacteria and automatically disinfect them as a precaution.

The Council will also hold an oversight hearing in September to examine the Mamdani administration's response and determine why residents lacked access to real-time information about cooling tower compliance during the outbreak.

Menin's proposed bill would establish a dedicated summer hotline so New Yorkers can get updated information during Legionnaires' outbreaks and would require the Health Department to mount public information campaigns similar to those used during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"We mourn their passing, and our thoughts are with their family and loved ones.""

Second Major Outbreak in Two Years

The current cluster follows a similar outbreak in Harlem last year that sickened 114 people and killed seven. That crisis prompted the City Council to pass a law requiring building owners to test for Legionella every 30 days during warm weather months, up from the previous 90-day requirement.

Since the Harlem outbreak, more than 250 cooling towers across New York City have been cited for Legionella testing failures, with more than half located in Manhattan. The city typically sees between 200 and 700 cases of Legionnaires' disease annually.

Health officials continue to advise anyone who spent time in the affected zip codes to seek medical attention if they develop flu-like symptoms, including fever, cough, shortness of breath, headaches or confusion, which can appear up to 14 days after exposure. Legionnaires' disease can be treated with antibiotics when caught early.
